name: Fazlur Rahman Khan
tagline: The man who taught skyscrapers to stand tall
story:
In 1955, a young engineer from Dhaka arrived in America with a government scholarship and a quiet obsession: why did tall buildings have to be so heavy? Fazlur Rahman Khan had grown up watching structures fight gravity with brute force — thick walls, massive cores, steel piled upon steel. At the Illinois Institute of Technology, he began sketching something radical. What if the building's skin could be its skeleton?

The architecture world dismissed him. A structural engineer from Bangladesh telling American firms they'd been building wrong for decades? But Khan didn't argue — he calculated. At Skidmore, Owings & Merrill, he developed the "tubular design" concept, where a building's exterior columns would form a rigid tube, carrying wind and gravity loads with a fraction of the steel. His colleagues thought it was elegant theory. He turned it into the 100-story John Hancock Center in Chicago, completed in 1969 — using less steel per square foot than many buildings half its height.

Then came his masterpiece. The Sears Tower (now Willis Tower), completed in 1973, stood as the world's tallest building for 25 years. Khan's "bundled tube" design — nine interconnected tubes rising to different heights — was so revolutionary that it redefined what was structurally possible. He had made the impossible economical. Every supertall building built since owes a debt to his thinking.

Khan died of a heart attack in 1982, at just 52, while returning from a project in Saudi Arabia. He never saw the full flowering of his revolution — the Burj Khalifa, the Shanghai Tower, the entire modern skyline. But every time you look up at a skyscraper that seems impossibly slender, impossibly tall, you're seeing the world Fazlur Rahman Khan imagined from a drafting table in Chicago, proving that the boldest structures begin with the quietest conviction.
